title: When Validators Don’t Trigger: A Paired Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Repair for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N = 600 task pairs) to test whether a deterministic validator–guided repair pipeline (generate→validate→repair) reduces high‑risk semantic misconfigurations relative to single‑shot LLM generation in intent→vendor‑configuration tasks. The run used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one sampled initial candidate per pair was produced and reused by both arms; the guarded arm could differ from baseline only if the deterministic validator rejected that candidate and an automated repair executed. Using gpt-5-mini as generator and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as validator, every shared initial candidate passed the validator in both baseline and guarded conditions (baseline = 600/600; guarded = 600/600). The paired absolute difference = 0.0 (95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). No automated repairs were invoked. Per the preregistration, a seeded 100‑case validator sensitivity audit was planned but was not executed for this confirmatory run; that omission limits claims about validator construct validity and sensitivity. We report the preregistered design, exact paired results from archived artifacts, clarify the scientific meaning of shared_initial_candidate semantics (it measures validator/repair trigger efficacy, not independent generator differences), and give design recommendations for future generate→validate→repair evaluations.

sections.introduction: High‑level intent translation into vendor‑specific device configurations is an increasingly explored NetOps automation task. Prior prototype systems and surveys recommend augmenting LLM generators with deterministic validators, tool calls, or repair loops to mitigate hallucinations and semantic errors [1]–[5]. However, published evaluations are heterogeneous in dataset scope, validator definitions, and generation semantics, leaving open how to measure the practical efficacy of generate→validate→repair workflows under adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents. We preregistered and executed a narrowly scoped paired confirmatory experiment to answer a precise estimand under an explicit generation contract: Under shared_initial_candidate paired semantics (one sampled initial generation per task reused by both arms), does a deterministic validator‑guided repair pipeline change the final validator outcome relative to accepting the single LLM generation? Important: shared_initial_candidate semantics make the paired contrast capable only of detecting validator/repair effects that alter the same sampled initial candidate; it does not measure independent per‑condition generator variability. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experiment executed on 600 intent→configuration pairs with archived artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded presentation of the null (ceiling) outcome that arises under shared_initial_candidate semantics; and (3) concrete design recommendations (sampling semantics, validator audits, adversarial stress) for future generate→validate→repair evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM‑based intent→configuration research demonstrates feasibility but commonly pairs generators with validators, retrieval, or tool augmentation to reduce errors [6], [7]. Broader surveys document hallucination taxonomies and self‑correction/tool‑augmentation approaches that can reduce specific error classes in other domains (e.g., clinical calculators, code generation) but emphasize dependence on validator/tool quality and dataset selection [3], [4], [8]. Constrained or neurosymbolic decoding approaches can enforce syntactic/semantic constraints at generation time, but their transfer to vendor CLI grammars and full semantic correctness remains an open engineering challenge [9], [10]. These prior findings motivated our preregistered generate→validate→repair confirmatory design with explicit generation semantics and deterministic validators.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary estimand: The study preregistration (autocand-2026-01-prereg-v1) defined a paired confirmatory estimand: the paired absolute difference in high‑risk semantic failure proportions (guarded − baseline), to be tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Sampling, task selection, and generation semantics: task_count = 600 pairs were deterministically selected by the adapter's challenging_workflow_stress_v1 rule; planned episodes = 1,200. Crucially, the preregistered adapter contract specified generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate: exactly one sampled initial generation per task was produced and reused unchanged by both baseline and guarded conditions; the guarded arm could invoke the deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and, if that validator failed, issue at most one automated repair attempt. Model and runtime record: the declared generator was gpt-5-mini; archived model configuration for executed calls records temperature = null/unset — null/unset is explicitly not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Planned but unexecuted confirmatory audit: the preregistration included a seeded 100‑case validator sensitivity/specificity audit; that audit was not executed as part of the archived confirmatory run and therefore no confirmatory sensitivity estimate for deterministic_netops_validator_v5 is reported here. Inclusion/exclusion and contamination controls followed the preregistered rules (public‑source requirement, provenance checks, algorithmic redaction of unsafe adversarial exemplars). Analysis: the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor produced exact McNemar p‑value and paired bootstrap CI using archived results (bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729).
sections.results: Execution accounting: the preregistered run completed to plan: planned_episode_count = 1,200; completed_episode_count = 1,200; complete_pair_count = 600; model_calls_used = 600 (one shared initial generation per pair per the shared_initial_candidate contract); failed episodes = 0. Primary outcomes (archived, exact): baseline_success_count = 600/600 (100%); guarded_success_count = 600/600 (100%); contingency counts: n11 = 600, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (paired_bootstrap_percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Repairs invoked: none—no guarded repairs executed because the deterministic validator accepted every shared initial candidate. Planned validator audit not executed: as noted in Methods, the preregistered seeded 100‑case validator audit was not executed; therefore the archived confirmatory results do not include an independent assessment of validator sensitivity/specificity and the possibility of an overpermissive validator (ceiling effect) remains an unresolved empirical limitation.
sections.discussion: Scientific interpretation: under shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded pipeline can change a paired outcome only if the deterministic validator rejects the same sampled initial candidate and a repair produces a validator‑passing configuration. Because the validator accepted all initial candidates, the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to demonstrate benefit; the observed null (ceiling) outcome therefore documents lack of validator rejections on the chosen task bank, not generator inferiority or superiority. Design recommendations: (1) choose generation semantics to match the estimand — use independent per‑condition generations when the goal is to measure generator‑level differences and use shared_initial_candidate semantics when the goal is to measure validator/repair trigger efficacy; (2) preregister and execute validator sensitivity audits (e.g., seeded held‑out cases or seeded adversarial perturbations) before confirmatory tests to detect overpermissive validators that create ceiling effects; (3) incorporate adversarially stressed or harder task partitions to elicit validator triggers and repair opportunities. Sampling and reproducibility note: archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset for the executed calls; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling. Limitations and scope: tasks were synthetic items from deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5, only a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used, and the preregistered 100‑case validator audit was not executed; these constraints limit generality and prevent concluding about validator construct validity beyond the archived pass/fail outcomes.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N = 600 pairs) under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing single‑shot LLM generation and a deterministic validator‑guided repair pipeline. Both arms passed the deterministic validator in all pairs (100% baseline and guarded), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0 (95% CI [0.0, 0.0], p = 1.0). No automated repairs were invoked. This result emphasizes that (a) generation semantics determine what a paired estimand measures (validator trigger effectiveness vs. generation differences), (b) validators must be audited to avoid ceiling effects that mask downstream protections, and (c) future experiments should use independent per‑condition sampling or harder/adversarial task banks when the scientific goal is to measure generator‑level advantages of constrained decoding or other interventions. All preregistration, execution, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived per the preregistered plan.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: baseline and guarded used the identical sampled initial generation per pair; thus the paired estimand measures validator/repair trigger effectiveness, not independent generator differences.

Validator construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 accepted all initial candidates in this run; without the preregistered seeded 100‑case validator audit (not executed) an independent sensitivity/specificity estimate is unavailable, creating the risk of an overpermissive validator producing a ceiling effect.

Task external validity: tasks were synthetic items generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 under the preregistered contamination and redaction rules; results may not generalize to diverse production device configurations or vendor idiosyncrasies.
Model and adapter scope: only the declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one adapter/validator instance were used; no claim of model‑class generality is made.

Sampling record: the archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is explicitly not evidence of deterministic sampling. Independent per‑condition sampling would be required to evaluate generator‑level effects.

Power assumptions violated: the preregistration's power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline failure rate (~10%). The observed baseline failure rate was 0%, so the preregistered minimal detectable effect (5 percentage points) and intended power interpretation do not apply to this execution.

Planned validator audit not executed: the preregistered seeded 100‑case validator audit was not executed as part of the archived confirmatory run; validator sensitivity therefore remains an unresolved limitation and a concrete recommendation for follow‑up work.
